facts.claim: ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) has a language model write its reasoning steps and its actions in turn, and the actions let it pull in information from outside sources, such as Wikipedia.
Anthropic calls a system a workflow when code paths written in advance orchestrate the model and its tools, and an agent when the model directs its own process and tool use.
Anthropic advises finding the simplest solution possible and adding complexity only when needed: agentic systems often trade slower, costlier runs for better task performance.
Agents suit open-ended problems where it is hard or impossible to predict how many steps the task will need.
At each step an agent needs ground truth from its environment, such as tool results, to judge its progress.
Agent runs commonly include stopping conditions, such as a maximum number of iterations, to keep control.
Agents can pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when they hit a blocker.
Greshake et al. (2023) showed that instructions planted in data an AI app later reads can take over what it does, against real systems such as Bing's GPT-4 chat, and found no effective defence yet.
Because agents act on their own, they cost more and their errors can compound, so Anthropic recommends extensive testing in sandboxed environments with guardrails.
In Anthropic’s research system, as reported in June 2025, agents typically used about 4 times as many tokens as chat, and multi-agent systems about 15 times as many.
Sub-agents work in parallel, each with its own context window, which compresses what the lead agent has to hold.
In June 2025 Anthropic reported that, on its own internal research eval, a lead Claude Opus 4 with Claude Sonnet 4 sub-agents outperformed a single Claude Opus 4 agent by 90.2%.
In Anthropic’s BrowseComp analysis, reported in June 2025, token usage by itself explained 80% of the variance in performance.
Context is a finite resource with diminishing returns: as it fills, the model's ability to recall information from it accurately decreases.

Compaction summarises a conversation that is nearing the context window's limit; the skill is choosing what to keep and what to drop, and compaction that is too aggressive can lose subtle but critical context.
Clearing old tool results is one of the safest, lightest forms of compaction.
With structured note-taking, an agent regularly writes notes that are kept in memory outside its context window.
Specialised sub-agents can handle focused tasks with clean context windows and return only a condensed summary of their work, often 1,000 to 2,000 tokens.
